questions.prompt: A team maps its assistant's data: the student database, the fee database and the hosted model. The assistant writes each request body, prompt included, to an application log. What should the map add?
options: Nothing, logs are technical data
The application log, as a store of personal data
Only the hosted model's own logs
A note that logs are exempt for debugging
questions.explanation: A log that keeps prompts holds whatever the prompts carry, so it is a store with the same obligations as a table.
misconceptions: Treats technical files as outside the law whatever they contain
Looks only at stores outside the organisation
Invents a debugging exemption the law does not have

questions.prompt: On a data flow diagram, the step "send prompt" goes to a model endpoint hosted outside the Kingdom. Which obligation must be written on that edge besides minimum content?
options: Notice at collection only
The breach notification deadline
The conditions for transfer outside the Kingdom
The right to correction
questions.explanation: Sending personal data to a party outside the Kingdom is a transfer, allowed only under the conditions of Article 29 and its regulation.
misconceptions: Puts a collection duty on a sending step
Confuses an incident duty with a routine flow
Picks a right that applies to stored records, not to this step

questions.prompt: A guardian who signed the enrolment contract asks the school assistant how many days her son was absent. Which legal basis fits answering her?
options: The contract the guardian is a party to
Consent, collected again for each question
Legitimate interest, because the data is sensitive
No basis is needed for a parent
questions.explanation: Processing in implementation of an agreement the data subject (here through the guardian) is a party to does not need separate consent.
misconceptions: Believes consent is the only basis
Reverses the rule: legitimate interest is never available for sensitive data
Thinks a family relationship replaces a legal basis

questions.prompt: A quality log of enquiries keeps the children's health notes. The school wants to keep it on its legitimate interest. What must change first?
options: Nothing, quality checks are a legitimate interest
The guardians must be told once a year
The log must move to another server
The health notes must leave the log
questions.explanation: Legitimate interest is available only when no sensitive data is processed; health data is sensitive.
misconceptions: Thinks any business reason is enough whatever the data
Replaces a condition on the data with a notice
Treats location of storage as the legal question

questions.prompt: A file of guardians' details was exposed on 3 March. The school learns of it on 20 March and expects harm to the guardians. Under the breach guide, by when must SDAIA be notified?
options: Within 72 hours of 3 March
Within 72 hours of 20 March
Within 30 days of 20 March
Only once misuse is confirmed
questions.explanation: The 72 hours run from the moment the controller becomes aware, when harm to the data or the data subjects is expected.
misconceptions: Starts the clock at the breach instead of at awareness
Uses the period for answering a rights request
Waits for proof of misuse, which the guide does not require

questions.prompt: A guardian asks the school for a copy of all data it holds about her daughter. Without an extension, how long does the school have to act?
options: Seven days
Ninety days
Thirty days
There is no limit
questions.explanation: The Implementing Regulation sets 30 days, extendable once by 30 days with prior notice and reasons.
misconceptions: Confuses it with a short cache period
Confuses it with a retention period
Believes rights requests have no deadline

questions.prompt: Which retention rule for an assistant's enquiry log is complete?
options: Keep the log as long as it is useful
Delete old rows when the disk is full
Ninety days
Ninety days from the enquiry date, then scheduled deletion of rows and backups
questions.explanation: A rule names the period, the event that starts it and the method of destruction, backups included.
misconceptions: Gives no period at all
Ties deletion to storage cost, not to purpose
Gives a period without a start or a method

questions.prompt: To answer "what is left to pay for my son?", which fields does the prompt need?
options: The fee balance, the child's first name and the message
The whole fee record and the guardian's national ID
The student file, so the model has context
The guardian's IBAN, in case of a refund
questions.explanation: The purpose needs the balance and a name to greet; every other field fails the actual-need test.
misconceptions: Keeps identifiers in case they help
Believes more context always improves the answer
Collects for a possible future need, which the guideline rules out

questions.prompt: Student numbers are replaced by HMAC codes and names are removed. The school keeps the key. Under the PDPL guideline, the result is:
options: Anonymous data outside the law
Personal data, because it can be linked back
Public data that can be published
Encrypted data that needs no protection
questions.explanation: Pseudonymised data stays personal data because additional information can link it to the person.
misconceptions: Equates removing names with anonymisation
Jumps from a privacy measure to a classification level
Treats a cryptographic step as an exemption

questions.prompt: A pseudonymised file keeps campus, grade, gender and exact date of birth. The school's website lists sports-day winners with the same four details. What is the main risk?
options: None, the file has no names
The website breaks copyright
A join on the four details re-identifies most children
The codes can be guessed without the key
questions.explanation: Quasi-identifiers together are close to unique per child, so joining with a public list puts names back on the records.
misconceptions: Thinks names are the only identifiers
Looks at the wrong legal question
Blames the codes when the leak is in the other columns

questions.prompt: After generalising birth date to birth year and grade to a band, the smallest group of identical quasi-identifiers holds one child. What does this mean?
options: That child can still be singled out; suppress or generalise further
The data is now anonymous
Generalisation failed for every child
The key must be rotated
questions.explanation: k = 1 means at least one record is unique on the quasi-identifiers, so it is still exposed even if the average risk fell.
misconceptions: Reads a lower average as no risk
Confuses one exposed child with a complete failure
Fixes the codes when the problem is the other columns

questions.prompt: Why is a plain SHA-256 hash of the student number a weak pseudonym?
options: SHA-256 is no longer secure
Hashes are too long to store
It cannot be joined across files
Anyone can hash every possible student number and look the codes up
questions.explanation: The space of student numbers is small, so an unkeyed hash is reversed by trying them all; a keyed hash prevents that.
misconceptions: Blames the algorithm rather than the missing key
Treats storage size as the privacy problem
Gets it backwards: hashes join well, which is the danger

questions.prompt: A member of staff wants to paste a guardian's message, with the child's name and a medical detail, into a public chatbot to improve the wording of a reply. Which instrument decides whether that is allowed?
options: The Open Data Policy
The Generative AI Guidelines
The Data Sharing Policy
No instrument; it is a matter of style
questions.explanation: The Generative AI Guidelines say what may be entered into generative AI tools: nothing classified Restricted or higher.
misconceptions: Thinks open data rules cover any data that leaves the organisation
Treats a person typing into a tool as sharing between entities
Believes drafting help is outside the rules because no system is built

questions.prompt: The school wants to publish its fee schedule as a machine-readable file anyone may reuse. Which instrument governs the release itself?
options: The Data Classification Policy
The Personal Data Protection Law
The Open Data Policy
The Generative AI Guidelines
questions.explanation: The Open Data Policy governs how Public data is released for reuse: open by default, machine-readable, free and licensed.
misconceptions: Stops at the level and misses the release rules
Applies a personal data law to a set with no personal data
Names an instrument about generative AI tools

questions.prompt: A fee-charging training company finds an instruction dataset under CC-BY-NC-4.0 and wants to tune its customer assistant on it. What does the licence allow?
options: Any use with attribution
Any use, because the data is public on the hub
Use after classifying the dataset as Public
No use in the company's commercial service
questions.explanation: NC means non-commercial: a fee-charging service is commercial use whatever the attribution.
misconceptions: Thinks attribution satisfies every Creative Commons licence
Equates downloadable with free for any use
Confuses a licence condition with a classification level

questions.prompt: A research partner asks for attendance data and adds "we may pass it to other research partners when needed". Under the Data Sharing Policy, which condition answers that line?
options: No onward sharing, written into the signed agreement
Encryption of the file before sending
Publication of the results after the study
A shorter retention period
questions.explanation: Onward sharing changes the purpose and the accountable parties; the agreement must forbid it or name each recipient.
misconceptions: Fixes a security weakness instead of a purpose problem
Confuses the data with the study's findings
Treats a destination problem as a duration problem

questions.prompt: A report joins a published price list with each customer's outstanding balance. Which level does the report take?
options: Restricted, the higher of its parts
Public, because the prices are published
Somewhere between the two levels
None until it is reviewed
questions.explanation: Combined data takes the highest level of its parts, and individual balances are Restricted.
misconceptions: Lets the public part set the level
Averages levels instead of taking the highest
Forgets that unclassified data is treated as Restricted

questions.prompt: An attendance summary by campus, grade and gender has 12 of its 95 cells with fewer than five students. Before suppression, what level fits it?
options: Public, because it holds no names
Secret, because it concerns children
Restricted, because small cells describe single children
Public once the column names are changed
questions.explanation: A cell of one or two students is those students' attendance; until small cells are suppressed or merged, the table holds personal data.
misconceptions: Thinks removing names removes the personal data
Over-classifies: Secret is for serious national or entity-level impact
Treats a cosmetic change as protection

questions.prompt: Under a rule that only Public data goes to hosted models and Restricted data without sensitive fields goes to a model served in-house, where may pseudonymised absence counts go?
options: To any hosted model
Nowhere at all
To a hosted model if the key stays in-house
To the in-house model only
questions.explanation: Pseudonymised data is still personal data and keeps its Restricted level; counts without notes are not sensitive.
misconceptions: Thinks pseudonymised means Public
Applies the sensitive-data branch to counts with no health content
Believes holding the key moves the data's level

questions.prompt: A free hosted model router does not say where prompts are processed. How should a team treat it when deciding what it may receive?
options: As processing in the Kingdom until shown otherwise
As a transfer outside the Kingdom
As exempt, because the service is free
As a matter for the provider alone
questions.explanation: If the location cannot be shown, the conditions for transfer cannot be shown to be met, so it is treated as abroad.
misconceptions: Puts the burden of proof the wrong way round
Thinks price changes the legal position
Shifts the controller's duty to the processor

questions.prompt: Under the national framework's scales, a harm is rated likely (3) and high impact (3). What is its level and band?
options: 6, medium
9, high
3, medium
12, high
questions.explanation: The level is likelihood times impact, 3 × 3 = 9, which falls in the 8 to 12 high band.
misconceptions: Adds the ratings instead of multiplying
Takes one rating as the level
Uses the wrong impact rating

questions.prompt: A harm is rated unlikely (2) with a catastrophic impact (4). Which band does the framework give it?
options: Catastrophic, because the impact is catastrophic
Medium
High
Low
questions.explanation: 2 × 4 = 8, the high band; only 16 is catastrophic.
misconceptions: Lets the impact alone decide the band
Misreads the band edges
Lets the low likelihood dominate

questions.prompt: An assistant drafts replies to parents; enquiries about health and custody go to staff before any reply. The team proposes sending those replies straight away and reviewing them later. How does the ethics risk tier change?
options: It does not change; the same model is used
It falls, because replies are faster
It becomes unacceptable at once
It rises towards high risk, with conformity assessments
questions.explanation: Removing human review on sensitive matters affecting children raises the risk to basic rights, which the principles treat as high risk.
misconceptions: Thinks the tier depends on the model, not the use
Confuses speed with lower risk
Jumps to a level reserved for prohibited uses

questions.prompt: After treatment, a harm is still rated high. What does the framework expect next?
options: Further treatment, or acceptance by someone with the authority, with a reason, and escalation
Deleting the harm from the register
Lowering the impact rating until it is medium
Waiting for the next annual review
questions.explanation: Residual risk is re-assessed; a risk outside the appetite is treated further or accepted at the right level and escalated.
misconceptions: Treats a register as a list of open tasks to close
Adjusts the rating to fit the wish
Leaves a known high risk unmanaged

questions.prompt: Why must a fairness threshold be set before the test is run?
options: Because the principles require a fixed value of ten points
Because tests cannot be rerun
So it cannot be fitted to the results
So the developer can choose it freely
questions.explanation: A threshold defines fair before the run; one chosen after the results can be set to pass whatever happened.
misconceptions: Invents a fixed number the principles do not set
Confuses timing with repeatability
Thinks the builder should set the bar for their own work

questions.prompt: To test whether an assistant serves Arabic and English writers equally, which test set is best?
options: Each question written in both languages, by the same guardian
Forty English questions and a translation of the replies
The questions guardians sent last month, in whatever language
Arabic questions in Modern Standard Arabic only
questions.explanation: Pairing makes the language the only difference; the Arabic side should include the varieties guardians write in.
misconceptions: Tests the translation, not the assistant
Mixes question difficulty with language
Leaves out the dialects real users write in

questions.prompt: A pilot reports 100% correct replies. All test questions were in English, but half the users write in Arabic. Which bias type does the report show?
options: Automation bias
Measurement bias
Evaluation bias
Exclusion bias
questions.explanation: The test set did not reflect the real users, so the score overstated how well the assistant serves them.
misconceptions: Confuses a test-set flaw with over-trust in outputs
Thinks the expected answers were wrong
Names a bias about leaving data out of training

questions.prompt: Which line at the foot of each reply meets the Generative AI Guidelines' transparency items?
options: "Sent by our digital service."
"This reply may contain errors."
"See our privacy policy."
"Drafted with AI. Write 'staff' to reach a person."
questions.explanation: It says the reply was produced with AI and offers a channel that does not go through the AI.
misconceptions: Thinks a brand name discloses AI use
Replaces a route to a person with a disclaimer
Hides the information where people must look for it

questions.prompt: A routing rule sends sensitive enquiries to staff. Why is the Arabic word for "fees" a poor keyword for it?
options: It is too long to match
It appears in routine fee questions, so every balance question would go to staff
Arabic words cannot be matched
Fee questions are never sensitive
questions.explanation: A keyword that routine questions use raises false alarms; the rule must separate a disputed fee from a question about one.
misconceptions: Treats length as the matching problem
Believes matching only works in English
Forgets that fee disputes are sensitive
